```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(message = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.asp = 0.65)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))
```

## Problem 1

I simulate independent, uniformly distributed birthdays and check whether
any birthdays are repeated. Each group size is simulated 10,000 times.

```{r birthday_simulation}
birthday_repeated = function(n_people) {
  birthdays = sample(1:365, size = n_people, replace = TRUE)
  return(length(unique(birthdays)) < n_people)
}

set.seed(2367)

birthday_summary =
  expand_grid(n_people = 2:50, iteration = 1:10000) |>
  mutate(shared_birthday = map_lgl(n_people, birthday_repeated)) |>
  group_by(n_people) |>
  summarize(probability = mean(shared_birthday))
```

```{r birthday_plot}
birthday_summary |>
  ggplot(aes(x = n_people, y = probability)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Number of people", y = "Probability of a shared birthday")
```

The probability increases with group size and is approximately 0.5 at
23 people. Larger groups have more possible pairs, making a shared
birthday more likely.

## Problem 2

I read each participant's file using `map`, extract the arm and subject ID
from the filename, and reshape the weekly observations into long format.

```{r import_longitudinal_data}
study_data =
  tibble(file_name = list.files("data", pattern = "\\.csv$")) |>
  mutate(
    observations = map(paste0("data/", file_name), read_csv),
    file_name = str_remove(file_name, "\\.csv$")
  ) |>
  separate(file_name, into = c("arm", "subject_id"), sep = "_") |>
  mutate(arm = recode(arm, con = "Control", exp = "Experimental")) |>
  unnest(observations) |>
  pivot_longer(
    starts_with("week_"),
    names_to = "week",
    names_prefix = "week_",
    values_to = "observation"
  ) |>
  mutate(week = as.integer(week))
```

```{r spaghetti_plot}
study_data |>
  ggplot(aes(
    x = week, y = observation,
    group = interaction(arm, subject_id), color = arm
  )) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~arm) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:8) +
  labs(x = "Week", y = "Observation", color = "Arm") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

Each line represents one participant. The experimental group generally
increases over time, while the control group fluctuates without a clear
upward trend. The groups are more separated by week 8, although individual
trajectories vary within each group.

## Problem 3

For each true mean from 0 through 6, I simulate 5,000 samples with
30 observations and standard deviation 5. Each sample is tested against
a null mean of zero using a two-sided t-test with significance level 0.05.

```{r t_test_simulation}
sim_t_test = function(mu) {
  sample_data = rnorm(30, mean = mu, sd = 5)
  t.test(sample_data, mu = 0) |>
    broom::tidy() |>
    select(estimate, p.value)
}

set.seed(2368)

test_results =
  expand_grid(true_mu = 0:6, iteration = 1:5000) |>
  mutate(results = map(true_mu, sim_t_test)) |>
  unnest(results) |>
  mutate(rejected = p.value < 0.05)

test_summary =
  test_results |>
  group_by(true_mu) |>
  summarize(
    power = mean(rejected),
    mean_all = mean(estimate),
    mean_rejected = mean(estimate[rejected])
  )
```

```{r power_plot}
test_summary |>
  ggplot(aes(x = true_mu, y = power)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:6) +
  labs(x = "True mean", y = "Proportion rejecting the null")
```

Power increases as the true mean moves farther from zero because larger
effects are easier to detect with sample size and variability fixed.
At a true mean of zero, the rejection rate is approximately 0.05;
this is the Type I error rate, rather than power against a false null.

```{r estimate_plot}
test_summary |>
  pivot_longer(
    c(mean_all, mean_rejected),
    names_to = "samples", values_to = "average_estimate"
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = true_mu, y = average_estimate, color = samples)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:6) +
  scale_color_discrete(labels = c("All samples", "Rejected null only")) +
  labs(x = "True mean", y = "Average estimated mean", color = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Across all samples, the average estimate is close to the true mean.
Among rejected tests, estimates are generally too large for small positive
true means: selecting significant results favors estimates farther from
zero relative to their standard errors. As power approaches one, nearly
all samples are retained, so the averages converge. At a true mean of zero,
positive and negative significant estimates cancel in expectation because
the test is two-sided.
